  (mild/Leray–Hopf) smooth solution; the L² conditions exclude the pressure/Galilean
  non-uniqueness u ↦ u + a(t), p ↦ p - a'(t)·x.
* Blow-up: sup_{[0,T)×ℝ³} |u| = ∞, which given local boundedness is limsup_{t↑T}‖u(t)‖_∞ = ∞.
* f = 0 gives u = 0, so the Claim is not trivial.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE017
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped ContDiff

abbrev E3 := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- Standard basis vector `e_i`. -/
def e (i : Fin 3) : E3 := EuclideanSpace.single i 1

/-- Divergence of a vector field on `ℝ³`. -/
def divg (v : E3 → E3) (x : E3) : ℝ := ∑ i : Fin 3, fderiv ℝ v x (e i) i

/-- Vector Laplacian `Σᵢ ∂ᵢ∂ᵢ v`. -/
def lap (v : E3 → E3) (x : E3) : E3 :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, fderiv ℝ (fun y => fderiv ℝ v y (e i)) x (e i)

/-- `f ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ³ × (0, ∞))` and `f(·, T) ≡ 0`. -/
def IsAdmissibleForce (T : ℝ) (f : ℝ × E3 → E3) : Prop :=
  ContDiff ℝ ∞ f ∧ HasCompactSupport f ∧ (∀ q ∈ tsupport f, 0 < q.1) ∧ ∀ x, f (T, x) = 0

/-- `(u, p)` is a smooth finite-energy solution of the forced 3D Navier–Stokes equations
(viscosity 1) on `[0, T)` with `u(0) = 0`, bounded on every `[0, t'] × ℝ³`, `t' < T`. -/
def IsSmoothNSSol (f : ℝ × E3 → E3) (T : ℝ) (u : ℝ → E3 → E3) (p : ℝ → E3 → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun q : ℝ × E3 => u q.1 q.2) (Set.Ico 0 T ×ˢ Set.univ) ∧
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun q : ℝ × E3 => p q.1 q.2) (Set.Ico 0 T ×ˢ Set.univ) ∧
  (∀ x, u 0 x = 0) ∧
  (∀ t ∈ Set.Ioo 0 T, ∀ x,
    deriv (fun s => u s x) t + fderiv ℝ (u t) x (u t x) + gradient (p t) x
      = lap (u t) x + f (t, x)) ∧
  (∀ t ∈ Set.Ico 0 T, ∀ x, divg (u t) x = 0) ∧
  (∀ t ∈ Set.Ico 0 T, MemLp (u t) 2 ∧ MemLp (fun x => fderiv ℝ (u t) x) 2 ∧ MemLp (p t) 2) ∧
  (∀ t' < T, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ t ∈ Set.Icc 0 t', ∀ x, ‖u t x‖ ≤ C)

/-- There is a force `f ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ³ × (0,∞))` vanishing identically at time `T` for which the
Navier–Stokes solution from rest is smooth on `[0, T)` and unbounded as `t ↑ T`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ T : ℝ, 0 < T ∧ ∃ f : ℝ × E3 → E3, IsAdmissibleForce T f ∧
    ∃ (u : ℝ → E3 → E3) (p : ℝ → E3 → ℝ), IsSmoothNSSol f T u p ∧
      ∀ C : ℝ, ∃ t ∈ Set.Ico 0 T, ∃ x, C < ‖u t x‖

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE017

title: Random Wang tiles
plain: (Corrected.) Draw n Wang tiles whose four edge colours are chosen uniformly at random from c colours, and let c grow with n ≈ λc². How likely is the set to tile the plane? Show the probability has a limit F(λ) and find the critical λ above which tiling is almost certain.
math: Let $T_1,\dots,T_n$ be i.i.d. Wang tiles, each with its four edge colours i.i.d. uniform in $[c]$ and no rotations allowed. Let $n=\lfloor\lambda c^2\rfloor$ and $c\to\infty$. Prove or disprove: $F(\lambda)=\lim_{c\to\infty}\Pr(\{T_i\}\text{ tiles }\mathbb Z^2)$ exists for every $\lambda>0$, and $\lambda_c=\inf\{\lambda:F(\lambda)=1\}=1$, i.e. $F(\lambda)=1$ for $\lambda>1$ and $F(\lambda)<1$ for $0<\lambda<1$ (as the first-moment heuristic suggests). Further goal: determine $F$ on $(0,\lambda_c)$.
review_note: A
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E018: Random Wang tiles
Informal statement: let $T_1,\dots,T_n$ be i.i.d. Wang tiles, each with its four edge colours i.i.d. uniform in
$[c]$, no rotations. Let $n=\lfloor\lambda c^2\rfloor$, $c\to\infty$. Prove $F(\lambda)=\lim_c\Pr(\{T_i\}$ tiles
$\mathbb Z^2)$ exists for every $\lambda>0$, and that $\lambda_c=\inf\{\lambda:F(\lambda)=1\}=1$ (prove or
disprove; the first-moment heuristic suggests 1). Determining $F$ on $(0,\lambda_c)$ is a further, unformalized goal.
Formalization notes:
* A tile is `Fin 4 → Fin c` (edges 0 = N, 1 = E, 2 = S, 3 = W). A tuple `T : Fin n → Tile` tiles ℤ² if some
  placement `f : ℤ × ℤ → Fin n` matches E of (x,y) with W of (x+1,y) and N of (x,y) with S of (x,y+1).
  Repeated tiles are harmless (the set {Tᵢ} tiles iff the tuple does).
* The probability is the exact uniform count over all c^{4n} tuples (finite type, so `Nat.card` is fine).
* Claim: for every λ > 0 the limit F(λ) exists, F(λ) = 1 for λ > 1, and F(λ) < 1 for 0 < λ < 1; this is
  exactly "F exists and λ_c = 1" (F(1) is left unconstrained). ¬Claim: the limit fails to exist for some λ,
  or λ_c ≠ 1 (including λ_c = ∞).
-/

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE018
noncomputable section

/-- `T` (a tuple of `n` Wang tiles over `c` colours) admits a valid tiling of `ℤ²`. -/
def Tiles {c n : ℕ} (T : Fin n → Fin 4 → Fin c) : Prop :=
  ∃ f : ℤ × ℤ → Fin n, ∀ x y : ℤ,
    T (f (x, y)) 1 = T (f (x + 1, y)) 3 ∧ T (f (x, y)) 0 = T (f (x, y + 1)) 2

/-- Probability that `n` uniformly random Wang tiles over `c` colours tile the plane. -/
def tileProb (c n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (Nat.card {T : Fin n → Fin 4 → Fin c // Tiles T} : ℝ) / (c : ℝ) ^ (4 * n)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ l : ℝ, 0 < l → ∃ L : ℝ,
    Filter.Tendsto (fun c : ℕ => tileProb c ⌊l * (c : ℝ) ^ 2⌋₊) Filter.atTop (nhds L) ∧
    (1 < l → L = 1) ∧ (l < 1 → L < 1)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE018

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
plain: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
math: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.
review_note: L
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E019: Period-doubling torus bundles
Informal statement: Let W_n ∈ {a,b}^{2^n} be the length-2^n prefix of the fixed point of
a ↦ ab, b ↦ aa (n ≥ 1), φ_n ∈ SL₂(ℤ) the product with a ↦ R = [[1,1],[0,1]], b ↦ L = [[1,0],[1,1]],
and M_n the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy φ_n (hyperbolic since W_n contains both
letters). Prove that lim vol(M_n)/2^n exists.
Formalization notes: hyperbolic volume is not in Mathlib, so vol(M_n) is encoded through
Guéritaud's theorem (Geom. Topol. 10 (2006)): M_ω for a cyclic word ω = ω₀…ω_{m−1} in {R,L}
containing both letters carries the Floyd–Hatcher layered triangulation with tetrahedra Δ_i,
i ∈ ℤ/m, Δ_i sitting between letters ω_i and ω_{i+1}; i is a hinge iff ω_i ≠ ω_{i+1}. Angle
structures are parametrized by w : ℤ/m → ℝ; with (a,b,c) = (w_{i−1}, w_i, w_{i+1}) the dihedral
angles of Δ_i are z = π − 2b and {x, y} = {a + c, 2b − a − c} (non-hinge) or
{b + a − c, b + c − a} (hinge); an angle structure is w with all of w_i, x_i, y_i, z_i > 0
(equivalently 0 < w_i < π/2, concavity at non-hinges, |w_{i+1} − w_{i−1}| < w_i at hinges).
vol(M_ω) = max over angle structures of Σ_i Λ(x_i)+Λ(y_i)+Λ(z_i), Λ the Lobachevsky function
(Casson–Rivin + Guéritaud: max attained in the interior, equals the hyperbolic volume). We use
sSup of the functional over the open polytope (equal to the max by continuity); it is bounded
above (Λ ≤ 0.51), and the claim additionally asserts the polytope is nonempty, so an empty set
cannot make the claim trivial. Letters: true = a ↦ R, false = b ↦ L; the formula is symmetric
in R ↔ L and in word reversal, matching volume invariance under these changes of convention.
Check: W₁ = ab gives the figure-eight knot complement, vol = 2.0298… at w ≡ π/3.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE019
noncomputable section
open Filter Topology

/-- The period-doubling substitution `a ↦ ab, b ↦ aa` (`true = a`, `false = b`). -/
def subst (ω : List Bool) : List Bool :=
  ω.flatMap fun c => if c then [true, false] else [true, true]

/-- `W n = σⁿ(a)`, the length-`2ⁿ` prefix of the fixed point. -/
def W (n : ℕ) : List Bool := subst^[n] [true]

/-- Lobachevsky function `Λ(θ) = −∫₀^θ log|2 sin u| du`. -/
def lob (θ : ℝ) : ℝ := -∫ u in (0 : ℝ)..θ, Real.log (2 * Real.sin u)

section
variable (ω : List Bool)

/-- Cyclic successor / predecessor of a tetrahedron index. -/
def nxt (i : Fin ω.length) : Fin ω.length := finRotate ω.length i
def prv (i : Fin ω.length) : Fin ω.length := (finRotate ω.length).symm i

/-- First dihedral angle of tetrahedron `i`. -/
def xAng (w : Fin ω.length → ℝ) (i : Fin ω.length) : ℝ :=
  if ω.get i = ω.get (nxt ω i) then w (prv ω i) + w (nxt ω i)
  else w i + w (prv ω i) - w (nxt ω i)

/-- Second dihedral angle of tetrahedron `i`. -/
def yAng (w : Fin ω.length → ℝ) (i : Fin ω.length) : ℝ :=
  if ω.get i = ω.get (nxt ω i) then 2 * w i - w (prv ω i) - w (nxt ω i)
  else w i + w (nxt ω i) - w (prv ω i)

/-- Third dihedral angle `π − 2 w_i`. -/
def zAng (w : Fin ω.length → ℝ) (i : Fin ω.length) : ℝ := Real.pi - 2 * w i

/-- `w` defines an angle structure on the layered triangulation of `M_ω`. -/
def IsAngleStructure (w : Fin ω.length → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i, 0 < w i ∧ 0 < xAng ω w i ∧ 0 < yAng ω w i ∧ 0 < zAng ω w i

/-- Volume functional `Σ Λ(x_i) + Λ(y_i) + Λ(z_i)`. -/
def volFun (w : Fin ω.length → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i, (lob (xAng ω w i) + lob (yAng ω w i) + lob (zAng ω w i))

/-- Hyperbolic volume of `M_ω` (Guéritaud: max of the volume functional). -/
def hypVol : ℝ := sSup (volFun ω '' {w | IsAngleStructure ω w})

end

def Claim : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∃ w, IsAngleStructure (W n) w) ∧
    ∃ L : ℝ, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => hypVol (W n) / 2 ^ n) atTop (𝓝 L)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE019

title: Is R(3,10) equal to 40 or 41?
credit: Radziszowski dynamic survey 'Small Ramsey Numbers'; Angeltveit (2023/2025).
premise_risks: Angeltveit's upper bound is computer-assisted; if it had an error the range would revert to 40-42
An unpublished construction or nonexistence proof could exist
plain: The Ramsey number R(3,10) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees either 3 mutual acquaintances or 10 mutual strangers. It is known to be 40 or 41, and nobody knows which. Settle it: either build a 40-vertex triangle-free graph with no 10 pairwise non-adjacent vertices, or show none exists.
math: Let $R(3,10)$ be the least $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains $K_3$ or an independent set of size $10$. Known: $40\le R(3,10)\le 41$. Decide whether there exists a triangle-free graph $G$ on $40$ vertices with $\alpha(G)\le 9$ (equivalently whether $R(3,10)=41$).
review_note: Known: Lower bound 40: Exoo (1989), a (3,10)-graph on 39 vertices. Upper bound 41: V. Angeltveit, 'R(3,10) <= 41', arXiv:2401.00392, Electron. J. Combin. 32(4) (2025) P4.30, improving 42 (Goedgebeur-Radziszowski 2013). Pandey-Ravi, arXiv:2601.03572 (Jan 2026), study structural properties of hypothetical critical graphs, quoting the older range 40-42 and assuming R(3,10)=42; they do not settle the value. No 2025-2026 resolution found.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E021: Is R(3,10) equal to 40 or 41?
The Ramsey number R(3,10) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees either 3 mutual acquaintances or 10 mutual strangers. It is known to be 40 or 41, and nobody knows which. Settle it: either build a 40-vertex triangle-free graph with no 10 pairwise non-adjacent vertices, or show none exists.
Informal statement: Let $R(3,10)$ be the least $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains $K_3$ or an independent set of size $10$. Known: $40\le R(3,10)\le 41$. Decide whether there exists a triangle-free graph $G$ on $40$ vertices with $\alpha(G)\le 9$ (equivalently whether $R(3,10)=41$).
Formalization notes: Claim says every graph on 40 vertices has a triangle or an independent set of size 10, i.e. R(3,10) <= 40. Given the known 40 <= R(3,10) <= 41: Claim true means R(3,10)=40, and ¬Claim (a triangle-free graph on 40 vertices with independence number <= 9 exists) means R(3,10)=41. Adjacency is irreflexive, so a triangle's vertices are automatically distinct.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE021
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin 40),
    (∃ a b c : Fin 40, G.Adj a b ∧ G.Adj b c ∧ G.Adj a c) ∨
    (∃ s : Finset (Fin 40), s.card = 10 ∧ ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, x ≠ y → ¬ G.Adj x y)
end OpenProblems.QEDE021

title: Four-colour triangle Ramsey number R(3,3,3,3)
credit: Radziszowski survey; Chung (1973); Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski (2004); Tatarevic (2026 preprint).
premise_risks: The bound 60 is an unrefereed 2026 preprint resting on unverified SAT runs; the safe published bound is 62
Problem may be stated with whichever upper bound the board accepts
plain: Colour every edge of a complete graph with one of four colours. How many vertices force a single-coloured triangle? The answer is known to lie between 51 and 60 (the 60 coming from a 2026 computer-assisted preprint), and is conjectured to be 51. Prove that 51 vertices already force one, or find a four-colouring of 51 vertices with no single-coloured triangle. Further questions (not part of the formal claim): any improvement of the upper bound, e.g. below 60, or a rigorous proof of 60.
math: Let $R_4(3)=R(3,3,3,3)$ be the least $n$ such that every 4-edge-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Known: $51\le R_4(3)\le 62$ (refereed), and $\le 60$ in a 2026 computer-assisted preprint. Claim: every 4-edge-colouring of $K_{51}$ contains a monochromatic triangle, i.e. $R_4(3)\le51$ and hence $R_4(3)=51$ (conjectured). Prove or disprove; a disproof is a 4-colouring of $K_{51}$ with no monochromatic triangle (giving $R_4(3)\ge52$). Further questions (not part of the formal claim): lower the upper bound (below 60, or confirm 60 rigorously).
review_note: Known: Lower 51: F. Chung (1973). Upper 62: Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski, Ars Combin. 72 (2004). Upper 60: M. Tatarevic, arXiv:2610.36648 (2026 preprint). It reduces to 296,081 SAT instances (UNSAT by Kissat and CaDiCaL); the reductions are in Lean/Mathlib, but the SAT exclusions are taken as a premise; extensive AI assistance is disclosed. Boza, arXiv:2603.10851 (2026), improves other multicolour bounds and cites 62 for R_4(3).

/-! QED-E022: Four-colour triangle Ramsey number R(3,3,3,3)
Colour every edge of a complete graph with one of four colours. How many vertices force a single-coloured triangle? The answer is known to lie between 51 and 60 (the 60 coming from a 2026 computer-assisted preprint). Narrow or close this gap.
Informal statement: Let $R_4(3)=R(3,3,3,3)$ be the least $n$ such that every 4-edge-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Known: $51\le R_4(3)\le 62$ (refereed), and $\le 60$ in a 2026 computer-assisted preprint. Improve either bound, i.e. exhibit a 4-colouring of $K_{51}$ with no monochromatic triangle, or lower the upper bound (below 60, or confirm 60 rigorously). Ultimately determine $R_4(3)$; it is conjectured to be $51$.
Formalization notes: Claim is the conjecture R_4(3)=51: every symmetric 4-colouring c of the pairs of Fin 51 has a monochromatic triangle on three distinct vertices (diagonal values c i i are irrelevant). namespace OpenProblems.QEDE022
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ c : Fin 51 → Fin 51 → Fin 4, (∀ i j : Fin 51, c i j = c j i) →
    ∃ i j k : Fin 51, i ≠ j ∧ j ≠ k ∧ i ≠ k ∧ c i j = c j k ∧ c i j = c i k
end OpenProblems.QEDE022

title: Does the Steiner system S(2,6,51) exist?
credit: Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Abel-Greig table); Banakh-Hetman-Ravsky (2025).

plain: Can you choose 6-element groups from 51 objects so that every pair of objects lies together in exactly one group (that would take 85 groups)? The arithmetic allows it, but no one has built one or proved it impossible. This is the smallest such undecided case for groups of size 6.

title: Ramsey multiplicity constant of K_4
credit: Erdos; Thomason; Parczyk-Pokutta-Spiegel-Szabo (2022/2024); Grzesik-Lee-Lidicky-Volec.
premise_risks: Asymptotic constant; Lean formalization would need the limit definition, and 'improve a bound' is not a yes/no claim
plain: In any red/blue colouring of the edges of a huge complete graph, some fraction of all 4-vertex sets must be single-coloured (all 6 edges the same colour). The minimum possible fraction is known only to lie between about 0.0296 and 0.03015. Pin it down further, or find its exact value.
math: Let $c_4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{G,|V(G)|=n}\big(k_4(G)+k_4(\bar G)\big)/\binom n4$. Known: $0.0296<c_4\le U=4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}<0.030145$ (Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó). Formal target: improve the upper bound strictly, i.e. prove $c_4<4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}$ (more generally improve either bound or determine $c_4$).
review_note: Known: Upper: Thomason (1989) < 1/33; Parczyk-Pokutta-Spiegel-Szabo, arXiv:2206.04036, Found. Comput. Math. (2024): c_4 <= 4551721·2^{-24}·3^{-2} < 0.030145 (blow-ups of a 768-vertex Cayley graph). Lower: Niess (arXiv:1207.4714) 0.0287; Sperfeld; Grzesik-Lee-Lidicky-Volec: c_4 > 0.0296 (cited in PPSS). Erdos's conjecture c_4 = 1/32 was refuted by Thomason.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E024: Ramsey multiplicity constant of K_4
In any red/blue colouring of the edges of a huge complete graph, some fraction of all 4-vertex sets must be single-coloured (all 6 edges the same colour). The minimum possible fraction is known only to lie between about 0.0296 and 0.03015. Pin it down further, or find its exact value.
Informal statement: Let $c_4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{G,|V(G)|=n}\big(k_4(G)+k_4(\bar G)\big)/\binom n4$.
Known: $0.0296<c_4\le U:=4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}\approx 0.0301449$ (upper bound:
Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó, Found. Comput. Math. 2024, from blow-ups of a 768-vertex Cayley
graph). Formalized target (strict improvement of the best known UPPER bound): prove $c_4 < U$.
Formalization notes:
* `mono G` counts 4-element vertex sets of `G` that are cliques of `G` or of its complement
  `Gᶜ` (i.e. the monochromatic K₄'s of the red/blue colouring "red = edge of G"). A 4-set cannot
  be both, so this is k₄(G) + k₄(Ḡ).
* `m n` = min over all simple graphs on `Fin n` of `mono G / C(n,4)` (an `iInf` over the finite,
  nonempty type `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`; values lie in [0,1], so the real `iInf` is a genuine
  minimum). For n < 4 the ratio is the junk value 0, which is irrelevant below.
* Standard averaging over (n−1)-vertex subsets shows `m n` is nondecreasing for n ≥ 4, so
  c₄ = lim m n = sup_{n≥4} m n exists and m n ≤ c₄ for all n ≥ 4. Hence
  c₄ < U  ⇔  ∃ c < U, m n ≤ c for all large n. We state the right-hand side, which avoids
  defining the limit with junk values. (A single finite graph can never prove it, as m n ≤ c₄;
  a proof needs a sequence, e.g. a better blow-up construction.)
* The known upper bound is non-strict (it is the exact density of a blow-up family), so
  `Claim` is a genuine strict improvement. Proving `Claim` = c₄ < 4551721/(2²⁴·9). Proving
  `¬Claim` = c₄ = 4551721/(2²⁴·9) exactly (the PPSS construction is optimal), given the known
  bound c₄ ≤ U.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE024
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Number of monochromatic 4-sets: 4-cliques of `G` plus 4-cliques of the complement. -/
def mono {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Fin n))).filter (fun s : Finset (Fin n) =>

/-! QED-E026: Total colouring of planar graphs with maximum degree 6
A total colouring colours both vertices and edges so that touching objects (adjacent vertices, edges sharing an end, an edge and its endpoint) get different colours. It is conjectured that Δ+2 colours always suffice, where Δ is the maximum degree. For planar graphs this is proved for every Δ except Δ=6: show every planar graph with maximum degree 6 has a total colouring with 8 colours.

Formalization notes:
* Graphs: finite simple graphs, w.l.o.g. on vertex set `Fin n` (every finite graph is isomorphic
  to one; all notions here are isomorphism-invariant).
* Planarity: by Wagner's theorem a finite graph is planar (has an embedding in the plane) iff it
  has neither K₅ nor K₃,₃ as a minor; we take this as the definition. Minors are given by branch
  sets: pairwise disjoint vertex sets each inducing a connected subgraph (Mathlib's `Connected`
  includes nonemptiness), with an edge between the branch sets of adjacent vertices of the minor.
* Maximum degree exactly 6: every vertex has at most 6 neighbours and some vertex has exactly 6
  (degrees as `Set.ncard` of the neighbour set, which is finite).

  `ce : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 8` (only values on edges matter) such that adjacent vertices get
  different colours, two distinct edges at a common vertex get different colours, and each edge
  differs from both its endpoints (the condition is stated for every ordered adjacent pair, so
  it covers both endpoints since `Sym2.mk (u,v) = Sym2.mk (v,u)`). This is exactly χ''(G) ≤ 8.

noncomputable section

/-- `H` is a minor of `G`: there are pairwise disjoint branch sets `B w ⊆ V`, each inducing a
connected (in particular nonempty) subgraph of `G`, with a `G`-edge between `B w` and `B w'`
whenever `w w'` is an edge of `H`. -/
def IsMinor {V W : Type} (H : SimpleGraph W) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : W → Set V,
    (∀ w : W, (G.induce (B w)).Connected) ∧
    (∀ w w' : W, w ≠ w' → Disjoint (B w) (B w')) ∧
    (∀ w w' : W, H.Adj w w' → ∃ x ∈ B w, ∃ y ∈ B w', G.Adj x y)

/-- The complete graph `K₅`. -/

/-- The complete bipartite graph `K₃,₃`. -/
def K33 : SimpleGraph (Fin 3 ⊕ Fin 3) := completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 3) (Fin 3)

def Planar {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ¬ IsMinor K5 G ∧ ¬ IsMinor K33 G


/-- A total colouring of `G` with colours `Fin k`. -/
def IsTotalColouring {n k : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (cv : Fin n → Fin k)
    (ce : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin k) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v : Fin n, G.Adj u v → cv u ≠ cv v) ∧
  (∀ u v : Fin n, G.Adj u v → ce (s(u, v)) ≠ cv u) ∧
  (∀ u v w : Fin n, G.Adj u v → G.Adj u w → v ≠ w →
    ce (s(u, v)) ≠ ce (s(u, w)))

  (∀ v : Fin n, (G.neighborSet v).ncard ≤ 6) ∧ ∃ v : Fin n, (G.neighborSet v).ncard = 6

def Claim : Prop :=

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE026

def mulOf {n : ℕ} (g : Group (Fin n)) (a b : Fin n) : Fin n :=

      (@DivInvMonoid.toMonoid (Fin n) (@Group.toDivInvMonoid (Fin n) g)))) a b

def IsoRel (n : ℕ) (g h : Group (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : Fin n ≃ Fin n, ∀ a b : Fin n, e (mulOf g a b) = mulOf h (e a) (e b)

def Claim : Prop := numGroups 2048 < 1780000000000000

end OpenProblems.QEDE037

title: The first decimal digit of the square-lattice site percolation threshold
credit: Wierman–Oberly 2024 (upper bound 0.666894); van den Berg–Ermakov 1996 (lower bound 0.556); Riordan–Walters 2007 (high-confidence numerics)
plain: Colour each square of an infinite chessboard black independently with probability p. Above a critical value p_c an infinite connected black region appears. Simulations put p_c at 0.592746..., and a randomised computer method certifies 0.5925 <= p_c <= 0.5930 with 99.9999% confidence. The best proved bounds, though, are only 0.556 < p_c < 0.666894, which do not even settle the first decimal digit. Prove that p_c < 0.6, so that p_c = 0.5...
math: Let $p_c=p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(\mathbb Z^2)=\sup\{p:\theta(p)=0\}$, where $\theta(p)$ is the probability under product Bernoulli($p$) site percolation on $\mathbb Z^2$ (nearest-neighbour adjacency) that the origin lies in an infinite open cluster. Prove, by a deterministic argument (computer assistance with exact or interval arithmetic allowed, statistical sampling not), that $p_c<3/5$. With the known $p_c>0.556$, this gives $p_c\in(0.5,0.6)$.
review_note: Known: Lower bound: p_c > 0.556 (van den Berg-Ermakov 1996), with no improvement found since. Upper bounds: 0.679492 (Wierman 1995, substitution method, CPC 4), then 0.666894 (Wierman-Oberly 2024, substitution method on self-matching lattices, the first improvement since 1995). Oberly-Wierman describe ongoing work on further small improvements by the same method. Non-rigorous: p_c = 0.59274605... from high-precision numerics (e.g. Jacobsen 2015 transfer matrices; Newman-Ziff Monte Carlo). Statistical: Riordan-Walters 2007, using the Balister-Bollobas-Walters 1-independent comparison method with Monte Carlo evaluation of a finite-box event, give [0.5925, 0.5930] at 99.9999% confidence. They note that exact enumeration of the needed box probabilities is impractical. Also p_c^site(Z^2) > 1/2 strictly (Higuchi) and p_c^site(Z^2) + p_c^site(matching lattice) = 1.
refs: J. C. Wierman, Substitution method critical probability bounds for the square lattice site percolation model, Combin. Probab. Comput. 4 (1995) 181-188.

J. C. Wierman, S. P. Oberly, A new upper bound for the site percolation threshold of the square lattice, in Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing (Springer, 2024), doi:10.1007/978-3-031-62166-6_9.
J. van den Berg, A. Ermakov, A new lower bound for the critical probability of site percolation on the square lattice, Random Structures Algorithms 8 (1996) 199-212.
O. Riordan, M. Walters, Rigorous confidence intervals for critical probabilities, Phys. Rev. E 76 (2007) 011110, arXiv:math/0702232.
P. Balister, B. Bollobas, M. Walters, Continuum percolation with steps in the square or the disc, Random Structures Algorithms 26 (2005) 392-403.
J. L. Jacobsen, Critical points of Potts and O(N) models from eigenvalue identities in periodic Temperley-Lieb algebras, J. Phys. A 48 (2015) 454003.

/-! QED-E038: The first decimal digit of the square-lattice site percolation threshold
Colour each square of an infinite chessboard black independently with probability p. Above a
critical value p_c an infinite connected black region appears. Simulations put p_c at 0.592746…,
and a randomised computer method certifies 0.5925 ≤ p_c ≤ 0.5930 with 99.9999% confidence, but
the best proved bounds are only 0.556 < p_c < 0.666894. Those bounds do not even determine the
first decimal digit of p_c. Prove that p_c < 0.6, i.e. that the first digit is 5.
Informal statement: Let $p_c=p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(\mathbb Z^2)$ be the critical probability for
Bernoulli site percolation on the square lattice (nearest-neighbour adjacency). Prove, by a
deterministic (non-statistical) argument, that $p_c < 3/5$. Together with the known lower bound
$p_c > 0.556$ this pins $p_c$ to $(0.5, 0.6)$, so its decimal expansion begins $0.5\ldots$.
Formalization notes:
* Configurations: `ω : ℤ × ℤ → Bool`, `ω x = true` meaning site x is open (black). The law
  `perc p` is Mathlib's infinite product measure `Measure.infinitePi` of Bernoulli(p) measures
  on `Bool` (`ProbabilityTheory.bernoulliMeasure true false p`, mass p on `true`), i.e. the
  product Bernoulli measure on {0,1}^(ℤ²) with the product σ-algebra. Parameters are taken in
  `unitInterval`.
* Clusters: sites are adjacent iff they differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate (ℓ¹ distance 1).
  The open cluster of the origin is the set of sites reachable from (0,0) along adjacent open
  sites (`Relation.ReflTransGen` of the open-adjacency relation; the step relation requires both
  ends open, so if the origin is closed its "cluster" is {0}). θ(p) = probability that this set
  is infinite.
* p_c := sup {p ∈ [0,1] : θ(p) = 0} as a real number. The set contains 0 (θ(0) = 0) and is
  bounded above by 1, so `sSup` is the usual critical probability (θ is nondecreasing).
* The number 3/5 is not a tuning knob: it is the coarsest bound that fixes a decimal digit, and
  the current rigorous interval (0.556, 0.666894) straddles 0.6. A proof must be a mathematical
  proof (possibly computer-assisted with exact arithmetic); a Monte Carlo confidence interval
  does not count. Proving `Claim` settles the problem. Proving `¬Claim` would mean p_c ≥ 0.6,
  contradicting all numerics.

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE038
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Site configurations on `ℤ²`. -/
abbrev Config : Type := ℤ × ℤ → Bool

/-- Nearest-neighbour adjacency on `ℤ²`. -/
def Adj (x y : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |x.1 - y.1| + |x.2 - y.2| = 1

/-- One step between adjacent open sites. -/
def OpenStep (ω : Config) (x y : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := Adj x y ∧ ω x = true ∧ ω y = true

/-- The open cluster of the origin is infinite. -/
def Percolates (ω : Config) : Prop :=
  {z : ℤ × ℤ | Relation.ReflTransGen (OpenStep ω) (0, 0) z}.Infinite

/-- Product Bernoulli(`p`) site percolation measure. -/
def perc (p : unitInterval) : Measure Config :=
  Measure.infinitePi (fun _ : ℤ × ℤ => bernoulliMeasure true false p)

/-- `θ(p)`: probability that the origin is in an infinite open cluster. -/
def theta (p : unitInterval) : ℝ≥0∞ := perc p {ω : Config | Percolates ω}

/-- Critical probability `p_c = sup {p ∈ [0,1] : θ(p) = 0}`. -/
def pc : ℝ := sSup {p : ℝ | ∃ hp : p ∈ unitInterval, theta ⟨p, hp⟩ = 0}

/-- The first decimal digit of `p_c` is 5: `p_c < 3/5`. -/
def Claim : Prop := pc < 3 / 5

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE038

/-- A packing of congruent copies of `K`: a sequence of isometries of `E` (rotations,
reflections, translations) whose images of `K` have pairwise disjoint interiors. -/
def IsPacking (K : Set E) (g : ℕ → (E ≃ᵢ E)) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≠ j → Disjoint (interior (g i '' K)) (interior (g j '' K))

/-- Fraction of the ball of radius `R` about the origin covered by the packing. -/
def coveredFraction (K : Set E) (g : ℕ → (E ≃ᵢ E)) (R : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=

title: No three in line: beat 3n/2
credit: Dudeney (1917); Hall–Jackson–Sudbery–Wild (1975); Guy–Kelly (1968)
premise_risks: the problem is famous (Dudeney); only the constant improvement is asked, not the 2n question
Epoch AI hosts a closely related target (1.8n, arbitrarily large n), so a solution may surface there first
plain: How many points of an n-by-n grid can you pick so that no three of them lie on one straight line (at any angle)? Each row holds at most two, so 2n is the ceiling, and explicit constructions from 1975 give about 1.5n for large n. Find, for all large n, a construction with at least cn points for some constant c > 1.5.
math: Let $f(n)$ be the largest size of $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}^2$ with no three collinear points. Known: $(\tfrac32-o(1))n\le f(n)\le 2n$. Prove there is $c>3/2$ with $f(n)\ge cn$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
review_note: Known: Lower $(3/2-o(1))n$: Hall, Jackson, Sudbery, Wild, JCTA 18 (1975). Upper $2n$ (pigeonhole); Guy–Kelly (1968) heuristic $f(n)\sim(\pi/\sqrt3)n\approx1.814n$. $f(n)=2n$ attained computationally for all $n\le46$ and some larger even $n$ (Flammenkamp); Epoch AI's page reports tightness for $n\le70$. For $k\ge3$, the no-$(k+1)$-in-line maximum is $kn$ for large $n$: arXiv:2607.05255 (July 2026), after arXiv:2502.00176 and arXiv:2510.17743; arXiv:2508.07632's randomised constructions are vacuous at $k=2$. Epoch AI lists 'more than 1.8n for arbitrarily large n' as an open problem.

/-! QED-E041: No three in line: beat 3n/2

def NoThreeCollinear (S : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ p ∈ S, ∀ q ∈ S, ∀ r ∈ S, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → q ≠ r →
    (q.1 - p.1) * (r.2 - p.2) ≠ (q.2 - p.2) * (r.1 - p.1)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, 3 / 2 < c ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n →
    ∃ S : Finset (ℤ × ℤ),
      (∀ p ∈ S, 1 ≤ p.1 ∧ p.1 ≤ (n : ℤ) ∧ 1 ≤ p.2 ∧ p.2 ≤ (n : ℤ)) ∧
      NoThreeCollinear S ∧ c * (n : ℝ) ≤ (S.card : ℝ)

end OpenProblems.QEDE041

Build a knot out of straight sticks joined end to end. The stick number of a knot is the fewest sticks that can make it. If all the sticks must also be the same length, you might need more. Is there any knot that really does need more sticks when they all have to be the same length?
Informal statement: For a knot type $K$ let $s(K)$ be the minimum number of edges of a polygonal knot in $\mathbb R^3$ of type $K$, and $s_{eq}(K)$ the minimum over polygons with all edges of equal length. Trivially $s_{eq}(K)\ge s(K)$. Is there a knot type $K$ with $s_{eq}(K)>s(K)$? (Formal `Claim`: yes. The alternatives — $s_{eq}=s$ for all $K$, or for an infinite family — are not separately formalized; $\neg$Claim is "$s_{eq}=s$ for all $K$".)
Formalization notes:
* Polygonal knots: a list `l` of vertices in ℝ³ (closed polygon, edge from the last vertex back
  to the first), embedded (`Simple`: ≥ 3 vertices and the PL parametrization `param` is
  injective on [0, n)). Every tame knot has polygonal representatives, so knot types = classes
  of polygonal knots.
* Knot type (`Iso`): equivalence closure of three elementary moves: cyclic relabelling
  (`rotate 1`), subdivision of the first edge at an interior point, and a straight-line slide of
  the first vertex along which every intermediate polygon is embedded. Rotation lets these act
  anywhere. Reidemeister's Δ-move (replace edge [a,b] by [a,c] ∪ [c,b] when the triangle abc
  meets the knot only in [a,b]) is a subdivision followed by a slide of the new vertex, and its
  inverse is in the closure. Conversely every move is realised by a PL ambient isotopy. So
  `Iso` is exactly PL ambient isotopy of oriented polygonal knots (Reidemeister 1927), which is
  the same as ambient isotopy of tame knots. Mirror images are not identified (no reflection
  move), and orientation is kept (no reversal move).

* Stick number `stick l` = least number of vertices (= edges) of a polygon `Iso` to `l`;
  equilateral stick number `eqStick l` = the same over equilateral polygons (all edges of the
  same length as the first). Both sets are nonempty for every knot (equilateral representatives
  exist for every knot type), so `sInf` is a true minimum. Orientation and mirror conventions
  are irrelevant here (reversal and reflection preserve edge counts and edge lengths), and
  `Iso` preserves embeddedness.
* Proving `Claim` = some knot has s_eq(K) > s(K). Proving `¬Claim` = s_eq = s for every knot.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE048
noncomputable section

/-- Points of `ℝ³` (Euclidean). -/
abbrev E3 : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- Vertex `k` of the closed polygon with vertex list `l` (indices taken mod the length). -/
def vtx (l : List E3) (k : ℕ) : E3 := l.getD (k % l.length) 0

/-- Piecewise-linear parametrization: on `[i, i+1]` it runs along the edge from vertex `i` to
vertex `i+1`; on `[0, n)` (n = number of vertices) it traverses the polygon once. -/
def param (l : List E3) (s : ℝ) : E3 :=
  (1 - (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ))) • vtx l ⌊s⌋₊ + (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ)) • vtx l (⌊s⌋₊ + 1)

/-- Double points of the polygon: parameter pairs `0 ≤ s < s' < n` with the same image. -/
def doublePts (l : List E3) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {q : ℝ × ℝ | 0 ≤ q.1 ∧ q.1 < q.2 ∧ q.2 < (l.length : ℝ) ∧ param l q.1 = param l q.2}

/-- A polygonal knot: at least 3 vertices and the closed polygon is embedded (this also forces
consecutive vertices to be distinct). -/
def Simple (l : List E3) : Prop := 3 ≤ l.length ∧ doublePts l = ∅

/-- The polygon `x :: r` with its first vertex moved to `(1-t)x + t x'`. -/
def movePath (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) (t : ℝ) : List E3 := ((1 - t) • x + t • x') :: r

/-- Elementary isotopy moves: cyclic relabelling, subdivision of an edge, and a straight-line
slide of one vertex during which the polygon stays embedded. -/
inductive Move : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | rot (l : List E3) : Simple l → Move l (l.rotate 1)
  | sub (x y p : E3) (r : List E3) : Simple (x :: y :: r) → p ∈ openSegment ℝ x y →
      Move (x :: y :: r) (x :: p :: y :: r)
  | slide (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) :
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, Simple (movePath x x' r t)) → Move (x :: r) (x' :: r)

/-- Same (oriented) knot type: the equivalence closure of `Move` (zig-zag chains). -/
inductive Iso : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | refl (l : List E3) : Iso l l
  | fwd {a b c : List E3} : Move a b → Iso b c → Iso a c
  | bwd {a b c : List E3} : Move b a → Iso b c → Iso a c

/-- All edges of the closed polygon have the same length. -/
def Equilateral (l : List E3) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : ℕ, k < l.length → dist (vtx l k) (vtx l (k + 1)) = dist (vtx l 0) (vtx l 1)

/-- Stick number of the knot type of `l`. -/
def stick (l : List E3) : ℕ := sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ l' : List E3, Iso l l' ∧ l'.length = n}

/-- Equilateral stick number of the knot type of `l`. -/
def eqStick (l : List E3) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ l' : List E3, Iso l l' ∧ Equilateral l' ∧ l'.length = n}

def Claim : Prop := ∃ l : List E3, Simple l ∧ stick l < eqStick l

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE048

title: Ropelength lower bound for the trefoil
credit: Denne–Diao–Sullivan (2006) bound; ropelength problem of Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan and Buck–Simon
premise_risks: The Schoen preprint is unrefereed and has several Zenodo versions; its claimed bound could be wrong, or have been raised in a newer version
Normalization: diameter convention (15.66 = 31.32 in radius convention)
16.372 is numerical, not a certified upper bound
plain: Tie a knot in a rope of thickness 1 using as little rope as possible. For the simplest knot, the trefoil, computer experiments find tight knots using about 16.37 units of rope. The last refereed proof shows that every knotted rope needs at least 15.66 units, and a 2026 computer-assisted preprint claims 15.76. Raise the proven lower bound for the trefoil substantially, ideally to 16.
math: For a $C^{1,1}$ closed curve, $\mathrm{Rop}=\mathrm{length}/(2\,\mathrm{reach})$; $R(3_1)=\inf$ over trefoils (attained). Known $15.66\le R(3_1)\lesssim16.372$ (refereed lower bound; numerical value), with an unrefereed 2026 computer-assisted claim $R(K)>15.7561$ for all nontrivial $K$. Formal target: $R(3_1)\ge16$.
review_note: Known: Lower: $\mathrm{Rop}\ge15.66$ for every nontrivial knot (Denne–Diao–Sullivan, Geom. Topol. 10 (2006), arXiv:math/0408026), improving 12 (Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan). Unrefereed: $\mathrm{Rop}(K)>15.75608926$ for every nontrivial $K$ via interval-arithmetic certificates (A. A. Schoen, 'Endpoint Tangents and a New Universal Lower Bound for the Ropelength of Nontrivial Knots', Zenodo, Sep 2026, v5.0.0, not peer reviewed). Klotz, arXiv:2611.14234 (Nov 2026), lists 31.51217852 (radius-normalized, so 15.756 diameter-normalized) for crossing number 3–8 as the current best, citing Schoen. Upper: numerical tight trefoil below 16.372 (DDS abstract). Minimizers exist (Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan 2002; Gonzalez–Maddocks–Schuricht–von der Mosel 2002).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E049: Ropelength lower bound for the trefoil
Tie a knot in a rope of thickness 1 using as little rope as possible. For the simplest knot, the trefoil, computer experiments find tight knots using about 16.37 units of rope. The last refereed proof shows that every knotted rope needs at least 15.66 units, and a 2026 computer-assisted preprint claims 15.76. Raise the proven lower bound for the trefoil substantially, ideally to 16.
Informal statement: For a $C^{1,1}$ simple closed curve $\gamma\subset\mathbb R^3$ let $\mathrm{Rop}(\gamma)=\mathrm{length}(\gamma)/(2\,\mathrm{reach}(\gamma))$ (length over tube diameter), and $R(3_1)=\inf\{\mathrm{Rop}(\gamma):\gamma\text{ a trefoil}\}$ (attained). Known: $15.66\le R(3_1)\lesssim16.372$ (refereed lower bound; numerical upper value), with an unrefereed 2026 computer-assisted claim $R(K)>15.7561$ for all nontrivial $K$. Formal target: $R(3_1)\ge16$.
Formalization notes:
* Curves: `γ : ℝ → ℝ³`, 1-periodic, C¹ with nowhere-vanishing derivative, injective on [0,1)
  (a regular embedded closed C¹ curve). Its image is `γ '' [0,1]`.
* Reach (Federer): sup of r ≥ 0 such that every point at distance < r from the image has a
  unique nearest point on it. For a closed C¹ curve, reach > 0 iff the curve is C^{1,1}, and the
  reach equals the thickness Δ[γ] (Gonzalez–Maddocks–Schuricht–von der Mosel); reach is finite
  for a closed curve, so the `sSup` is a real supremum. Curves of reach 0 have infinite
  ropelength and are excluded explicitly (avoiding the junk value x/0 = 0).
* Length = ∫₀¹ |γ'(t)| dt; Rop = length / (2·reach) (diameter convention, matching 15.66).
* Knot type: γ is a trefoil iff for all large N the inscribed polygon γ(0), γ(1/N), …,
  γ((N−1)/N) is a polygonal trefoil. For a regular embedded C¹ closed curve the inscribed
  polygons are, for N large, embedded and isotopic to γ, so this is the knot type of γ.
* Polygonal knots: a list `l` of vertices in ℝ³ (closed polygon, edge from the last vertex back
  to the first), embedded (`Simple`: ≥ 3 vertices and the PL parametrization `param` is
  injective on [0, n)). Every tame knot has polygonal representatives, so knot types = classes
  of polygonal knots.
* Knot type (`Iso`): equivalence closure of three elementary moves: cyclic relabelling
  (`rotate 1`), subdivision of the first edge at an interior point, and a straight-line slide of
  the first vertex along which every intermediate polygon is embedded. Rotation lets these act
  anywhere. Reidemeister's Δ-move (replace edge [a,b] by [a,c] ∪ [c,b] when the triangle abc
  meets the knot only in [a,b]) is a subdivision followed by a slide of the new vertex, and its
  inverse is in the closure. Conversely every move is realised by a PL ambient isotopy. So
  `Iso` is exactly PL ambient isotopy of oriented polygonal knots (Reidemeister 1927), which is
  the same as ambient isotopy of tame knots. Mirror images are not identified (no reflection
  move), and orientation is kept (no reversal move).

* `trefoil`: 12 integer points sampled from the (2,3) torus knot and rounded. Checked
  numerically: the polygon is embedded (minimum distance between non-adjacent edges ≈ 12.8,
  much larger than the rounding error) and a generic projection has 5 crossings with knot
  determinant 3; the only knot of crossing number ≤ 5 with determinant 3 is the trefoil.
* Choice of target: a bound just beyond 15.7561 might already be settled by the unrefereed 2026
  preprint (which claims Rop > 15.7561 for every nontrivial knot), so the formal target is the
  substantial bound R(3₁) ≥ 16. Known bounds: 15.66 ≤ R(3₁) (refereed), unrefereed claim
  R(3₁) > 15.7561, and numerically R(3₁) ≈ 16.372. The infimum R(3₁) is attained, so R(3₁) ≥ 16
  is exactly "every trefoil has ropelength ≥ 16". Proving `Claim` = R(3₁) ≥ 16. Proving `¬Claim`
  = some trefoil has ropelength < 16 (which would contradict the numerics, ≈ 16.372).
-/

noncomputable section

/-- Points of `ℝ³` (Euclidean). -/

/-- Vertex `k` of the closed polygon with vertex list `l` (indices taken mod the length). -/
def vtx (l : List E3) (k : ℕ) : E3 := l.getD (k % l.length) 0

/-- Piecewise-linear parametrization: on `[i, i+1]` it runs along the edge from vertex `i` to
vertex `i+1`; on `[0, n)` (n = number of vertices) it traverses the polygon once. -/
def param (l : List E3) (s : ℝ) : E3 :=
  (1 - (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ))) • vtx l ⌊s⌋₊ + (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ)) • vtx l (⌊s⌋₊ + 1)

/-- Double points of the polygon: parameter pairs `0 ≤ s < s' < n` with the same image. -/
def doublePts (l : List E3) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {q : ℝ × ℝ | 0 ≤ q.1 ∧ q.1 < q.2 ∧ q.2 < (l.length : ℝ) ∧ param l q.1 = param l q.2}

/-- A polygonal knot: at least 3 vertices and the closed polygon is embedded (this also forces
consecutive vertices to be distinct). -/
def Simple (l : List E3) : Prop := 3 ≤ l.length ∧ doublePts l = ∅

/-- The polygon `x :: r` with its first vertex moved to `(1-t)x + t x'`. -/
def movePath (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) (t : ℝ) : List E3 := ((1 - t) • x + t • x') :: r

/-- Elementary isotopy moves: cyclic relabelling, subdivision of an edge, and a straight-line
slide of one vertex during which the polygon stays embedded. -/
inductive Move : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | rot (l : List E3) : Simple l → Move l (l.rotate 1)
  | sub (x y p : E3) (r : List E3) : Simple (x :: y :: r) → p ∈ openSegment ℝ x y →
      Move (x :: y :: r) (x :: p :: y :: r)
  | slide (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) :
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, Simple (movePath x x' r t)) → Move (x :: r) (x' :: r)

/-- Same (oriented) knot type: the equivalence closure of `Move` (zig-zag chains). -/
inductive Iso : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | refl (l : List E3) : Iso l l
  | fwd {a b c : List E3} : Move a b → Iso b c → Iso a c
  | bwd {a b c : List E3} : Move b a → Iso b c → Iso a c

/-- A trefoil (of one chirality): 12 integer points on the (2,3) torus knot
`((2 + cos 3t) cos 2t, (2 + cos 3t) sin 2t, sin 3t)`, `t = 2πk/12`, scaled by 10 and rounded. -/
def trefoil : List E3 :=
  [!₂[(30 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), 9, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), -26, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, 10], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), 26, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), -9, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, -10]]

/-- A regular embedded closed `C¹` curve with period 1. -/
def IsClosedCurve (γ : ℝ → E3) : Prop :=
  ContDiff ℝ 1 γ ∧ (∀ t : ℝ, γ (t + 1) = γ t) ∧ (∀ t : ℝ, deriv γ t ≠ 0) ∧
    Set.InjOn γ (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1)

/-- Federer's reach of a set. -/
def reach (S : Set E3) : ℝ :=
  sSup {r : ℝ | 0 ≤ r ∧ ∀ x : E3, Metric.infDist x S < r →
    ∃! y : E3, y ∈ S ∧ dist x y = Metric.infDist x S}

/-- Length of a 1-periodic `C¹` curve. -/
def curveLength (γ : ℝ → E3) : ℝ := ∫ t in (0 : ℝ)..1, ‖deriv γ t‖

/-- The curve has the knot type of the trefoil. -/
def IsTrefoil (γ : ℝ → E3) : Prop :=
  ∃ N₀ : ℕ, ∀ N : ℕ, N₀ ≤ N → Iso (List.ofFn fun k : Fin N => γ (((k : ℕ) : ℝ) / (N : ℝ))) trefoil

/-- `R(3₁) ≥ 16`: every (thick) trefoil has ropelength at least 16. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ γ : ℝ → E3, IsClosedCurve γ → IsTrefoil γ → 0 < reach (γ '' Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) →
    (16 : ℝ) ≤ curveLength γ / (2 * reach (γ '' Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE049

title: Does Antihydra halt?
credit: bbchallenge community (Antihydra found 2024; reformulation by mxdys et al.); Ligocki, 'BB(6) is Hard (Antihydra)'
premise_risks: The TM ⇔ arithmetic equivalence rests on bbchallenge wiki and its formal proofs, not a refereed paper. M is self-contained either way.
Collatz-like; likely far beyond current methods
plain: Start with 8 and repeatedly multiply by 3/2, rounding down. Keep score: +2 for every even number you see and −1 for every odd number. Does the score ever go negative? This is exactly the question of whether a specific 6-state Turing machine, called Antihydra, ever halts. Answering it is the first obstacle to determining the sixth Busy Beaver number.
math: Let $a_0=8$ and $a_{n+1}=\lfloor 3a_n/2\rfloor$. For $n\ge1$ let $E_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ even}\}$ and $O_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ odd}\}$. Does there exist $n$ with $O_n>2E_n$? Equivalently (bbchallenge), does the 6-state 2-symbol Turing machine 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA halt from a blank tape? The conjecture is that it never halts.
review_note: Known: Simulated to $2^{38}$ rule steps without halting (bbchallenge wiki). Under a random-walk heuristic (steps +2/−1), the chance of ever reaching −1 from the current score is about $10^{-2.87\times10^{10}}$ (wiki). It is listed as an undecided 'probviously non-halting' cryptid on the BB(6) wiki page; the current BB(6) champion exceeds $10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow8$ (mxdys, June 2025). BB(5) is determined (arXiv:2509.12337). Related: Mahler's 3/2 problem; Dubickas on integer sequences from linear maps. More BB(6) cryptids, all unresolved: arXiv:2610.22603 (2026).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E050: Does Antihydra halt?
Start with 8 and repeatedly replace a by ⌊3a/2⌋. Score +2 for each even term and −1 for each odd term. Does the running score ever go negative?
Informal statement: With a₀ = 8, a_{n+1} = ⌊3aₙ/2⌋, E_n = #{i < n : aᵢ even}, O_n = #{i < n : aᵢ odd}, is O_n ≤ 2E_n for every n? (Equivalently, the 6-state TM 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA never halts, per the bbchallenge wiki.)
Formalization notes: `a` is the Hydra/Antihydra orbit with ℕ floor division. The score after n terms is 2·E n − O n; since it moves by +2 or −1, it goes negative iff it hits −1, iff O n > 2·E n for some n. `Claim` = "Antihydra never halts" (the conjectured answer). `¬Claim` = Antihydra halts. The TM equivalence itself is not formalized.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE050

/-- The Antihydra orbit: a₀ = 8, a_{n+1} = ⌊3aₙ/2⌋. -/
def a : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 8
  | n + 1 => 3 * a n / 2

/-- Number of even terms among a₀, …, a_{n-1}. -/
def E (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i : ℕ => Even (a i))).card

/-- Number of odd terms among a₀, …, a_{n-1}. -/
def O (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i : ℕ => ¬ Even (a i))).card

/-- Antihydra never halts. -/
def Claim : Prop := ∀ n : ℕ, O n ≤ 2 * E n

end OpenProblems.QEDE050

title: Translational tiling of the plane with two tiles: decidable?
credit: Yang & Zhang, arXiv 2506.19295 (open problem stated); Abel et al., arXiv 2509.07906 (Table 3)
premise_risks: Fast-moving area (k went 5→4→3 in 2025, and the 3D monotile in 2026); a late-2026 preprint could settle k=2
Connected vs. possibly-disconnected tiles may differ; the main statement allows arbitrary finite tiles
plain: You are given two shapes made of grid squares, and you may only slide copies of them around, never rotate them. Can copies of the two shapes cover the whole infinite grid with no gaps or overlaps? With one shape there is an algorithm that always answers this. With three shapes, one of them in several pieces, it was proved in 2025 that no algorithm can exist. Two shapes is the open case.
math: Given finite $F_1,F_2\subset\mathbb Z^2$, decide whether there exist $A_1,A_2\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ with $(F_1+A_1)\sqcup(F_2+A_2)=\mathbb Z^2$, i.e. every point of $\mathbb Z^2$ lies in exactly one translate $F_j+a$, $a\in A_j$. Is this problem decidable? (Variant: also require $F_1,F_2$ to be connected polyominoes.)
review_note: Known: k=1: decidable (Beauquier–Nivat 1991 for polyominoes; Bhattacharya 2020, periodic tiling conjecture in $\mathbb Z^2$, for arbitrary finite $F$). k=3: co-RE-complete with three polyominoes, one disconnected and two connected of constant size; two trominoes suffice for a periodic subset of 2D (Abel, Akitaya, Chung, Demaine et al., 'Undecidability of Tiling with a Tromino', arXiv:2509.07906, 2025; Table 3 lists 2D/2 pieces/translation as OPEN). k=4, possibly disconnected: Yang–Zhang, arXiv:2506.19295 (2025), who list the two-tile case as open. k=5 connected: Kim, arXiv:2508.10067. Two tiles in $\mathbb Z^2\times G_0$: undecidable (Greenfeld–Tao, arXiv:2108.07902). With rotations, two tiles: undecidable (arXiv:2506.11628). A single polycube in 3D, translations only: undecidable (arXiv:2610.12392, Oct 2026).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E051: Translational tiling of the plane with two tiles: decidable?
Given two finite sets of grid cells, can translated copies (no rotations) of them tile ℤ² exactly? Is there an algorithm deciding this?
Informal statement: Is the set of pairs (F₁, F₂) of finite subsets of ℤ² such that ℤ² = (F₁ + A₁) ⊔ (F₂ + A₂) for some A₁, A₂ ⊆ ℤ² decidable?
Formalization notes: Tiles are given as lists of cells in ℕ × ℕ (every finite subset of ℤ² can be translated into the first quadrant, and tileability is translation invariant, so this loses nothing). Duplicates in a list are harmless (`cells` is a set). `TwoTiles F₁ F₂` says every z ∈ ℤ² lies in exactly one placed copy, where a copy is a pair (tile index, translation vector) with the vector in the corresponding Aⱼ. That is a disjoint exact cover. An empty tile is allowed (the instance then degenerates to one-tile tiling, which is decidable, so it creates no loophole). `Claim` = the problem is decidable (computable in Mathlib's Partrec sense). `¬Claim` = undecidable. The connected-polyomino variant is not encoded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE051

/-- The cells of a tile, as a subset of ℤ². -/
def cells (F : List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {z | ∃ p ∈ F, z = ((p.1 : ℤ), (p.2 : ℤ))}

/-- Translates of `F₁` and `F₂` tile ℤ² exactly. -/
def TwoTiles (F₁ F₂ : List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ A₁ A₂ : Set (ℤ × ℤ), ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, ∃! q : Bool × (ℤ × ℤ),
    (q.1 = false ∧ q.2 ∈ A₁ ∧ z - q.2 ∈ cells F₁) ∨
    (q.1 = true ∧ q.2 ∈ A₂ ∧ z - q.2 ∈ cells F₂)

/-- Two-tile translational tiling of the plane is decidable. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ComputablePred (fun F : List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ) => TwoTiles F.1 F.2)

end OpenProblems.QEDE051

title: A polyomino of odd order
credit: Golomb / Klarner rectifiable-polyomino program; Stewart & Wormstein (1992); Reid
premise_risks: Reflections allowed (Golomb's convention); a rotations-only version could differ
Reid's rectifiable-polyomino page (not loaded) might list an odd-order example. OEIS says none is known.
plain: Some shapes made of squares, like the L-tetromino, can tile a rectangle. The order of such a shape is the fewest copies that can do it. Apart from rectangles themselves (order 1), every shape with a known order needs an even number of copies, and order 3 is proved impossible. Is there a non-rectangular polyomino whose order is odd?
math: For a polyomino $P$ that tiles some rectangle with congruent copies (rotations and reflections allowed), let $\mathrm{ord}(P)$ be the minimum number of copies in such a tiling. Does there exist a non-rectangular $P$ with $\mathrm{ord}(P)$ odd? First test case: $\mathrm{ord}(P)=5$.
review_note: Known: Order 3 is impossible: Stewart & Wormstein, 'Polyominoes of order 3 do not exist', JCTA 61 (1992) 130–136. Maltby, 'Trisecting a rectangle', JCTA 66 (1994): no non-rectangular 3-piece congruent dissection; M. Reid noted on math-fun that the 5-, 7- and 9-piece dissection cases remain open. Odd tilings, as opposed to odd minimal tilings, exist: Reid, 'Many L-shaped polyominoes have odd rectangular packings', Ann. Comb. 18 (2014) 341–357. OEIS A126140 (maximum order for n cells): 'No example of a non-rectangular polyomino is known for which its order is odd.'

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E053: A polyomino of odd order
Is there a non-rectangular polyomino whose order (fewest congruent copies tiling some rectangle) is odd?
Informal statement: For a polyomino P that tiles a rectangle with congruent copies (rotations and reflections allowed), ord(P) is the least number of copies in such a tiling. Does some non-rectangular P have ord(P) odd?
Formalization notes: Cells are points of ℤ × ℤ (unit squares indexed by lower-left corner). A polyomino is a nonempty finite cell set connected under edge-adjacency (|dx| + |dy| = 1). A congruent copy is the image under one of the 8 symmetries of ℤ² (optional coordinate swap, then signs e₁, e₂ ∈ ℤˣ = {±1}) followed by a translation; `place g` is injective, so a single copy never overlaps itself. `TilesRectWith P k` says k copies exactly partition an a × b rectangle with a, b ≥ 1 (cover plus pairwise disjointness). k = 0 is impossible because the rectangle is nonempty, and the empty set is excluded by `IsPolyomino`. `IsRect P` says P is a translate of an a × b rectangle, a, b ≥ 1. `Claim` = such an odd-order polyomino exists. `¬Claim` = every non-rectangular rectifiable polyomino has even order (or tiles no rectangle).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE053

/-- The a × b rectangle [0,a) × [0,b) of cells. -/
def rect (a b : ℕ) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) := {z | 0 ≤ z.1 ∧ z.1 < a ∧ 0 ≤ z.2 ∧ z.2 < b}

/-- `P` is a translate of a nonempty rectangle. -/
def IsRect (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b : ℕ) (t : ℤ × ℤ), 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, z ∈ P ↔ z - t ∈ rect a b

/-- Edge-adjacent cells. -/
def Adj (p q : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |p.1 - q.1| + |p.2 - q.2| = 1

/-- `P` is a polyomino: nonempty and edge-connected. -/
def IsPolyomino (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  P.Nonempty ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, ∀ q ∈ P,
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun x y : ℤ × ℤ => x ∈ P ∧ y ∈ P ∧ Adj x y) p q

/-- A symmetry of ℤ² (swap flag, two signs, translation) applied to a cell. -/
def place (g : Bool × ℤˣ × ℤˣ × (ℤ × ℤ)) (p : ℤ × ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  ((g.2.1 : ℤ) * (if g.1 then p.2 else p.1) + g.2.2.2.1,
   (g.2.2.1 : ℤ) * (if g.1 then p.1 else p.2) + g.2.2.2.2)

/-- `k` congruent copies of `P` exactly tile some nonempty rectangle. -/
def TilesRectWith (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b : ℕ) (c : Fin k → Bool × ℤˣ × ℤˣ × (ℤ × ℤ)), 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧
    (∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, z ∈ rect a b ↔ ∃ i : Fin k, ∃ p ∈ P, place (c i) p = z) ∧
    (∀ (i j : Fin k) (p q : ℤ × ℤ), p ∈ P → q ∈ P →
      place (c i) p = place (c j) q → i = j)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), IsPolyomino P ∧ ¬ IsRect P ∧
    ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ TilesRectWith P k ∧ ∀ k' : ℕ, k' < k → ¬ TilesRectWith P k'

end OpenProblems.QEDE053

title: Is Grundy's game eventually periodic?
credit: Berlekamp, Conway & Guy, Winning Ways; computations by A. Flammenkamp
premise_risks: Computed range: '239' and '235' are superscript-lost renderings (2^39 and 2^35 most likely); not verified from a clean source
Classic problem with no clear modern angle
plain: In Grundy's game, players take turns splitting a pile of coins into two smaller piles of different sizes, and whoever cannot move loses. The game's theory reduces to one number per pile size, its Grundy value. These values have been computed for piles of hundreds of billions of coins and show no repeating pattern yet, though Berlekamp, Conway and Guy conjectured that they eventually repeat. Do they?
math: Let $g(0)=g(1)=g(2)=0$ and for $n\ge3$ let $g(n)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(a)\oplus g(b): a+b=n,\ 1\le a<b\}$, where $\oplus$ is bitwise XOR. Is $g$ eventually periodic, i.e. are there $N,p\ge1$ with $g(n+p)=g(n)$ for all $n\ge N$? (Weaker open question: is $g$ bounded?)
review_note: Known: Berlekamp–Conway–Guy (Winning Ways) conjecture eventual periodicity; Wikipedia says it is unresolved. Flammenkamp's octal-games page, Table 2 entry for Grundy's game: values computed for all n up to '239', most likely $2^{39}$ with the superscript lost. The largest known value is 297, attained at n = 21544358589, and 1287 rare values are known, the largest at 48399022. Wikipedia's text reads 'first 235 values', most likely $2^{35}$. OEIS A002188. Golomb's periodicity for finite subtraction games does not apply.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E054: Is Grundy's game eventually periodic?
In Grundy's game a move splits a heap into two nonempty heaps of different sizes. Is the sequence of Grundy values of single heaps eventually periodic?
Informal statement: Let g(n) = mex{ g(a) ⊕ g(b) : a + b = n, 1 ≤ a < b } (so g(0) = g(1) = g(2) = 0). Are there N and p ≥ 1 with g(n + p) = g(n) for all n ≥ N?
Formalization notes: Instead of defining g by well-founded recursion, `IsGrundy g` states the mex recursion: no option value equals g n, and every smaller value is an option value. A function satisfying it exists and is unique (strong induction on n), so quantifying over all such g is neither vacuous nor ambiguous. ⊕ is `^^^` (bitwise xor on ℕ). For n ≤ 2 there are no options, which forces g n = 0. `Claim` = eventual periodicity (the Berlekamp–Conway–Guy conjecture). `¬Claim` = not eventually periodic.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE054

/-- `g` satisfies the Grundy-value recursion of Grundy's game. -/
def IsGrundy (g : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ,
    (∀ a b : ℕ, 1 ≤ a → a < b → a + b = n → g n ≠ (g a ^^^ g b)) ∧
    (∀ m : ℕ, m < g n → ∃ a b : ℕ, 1 ≤ a ∧ a < b ∧ a + b = n ∧ (g a ^^^ g b) = m)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ g : ℕ → ℕ, IsGrundy g →
    ∃ N p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → g (n + p) = g n

end OpenProblems.QEDE054

title: Do minimum-order k-chromatic graphs of girth at least g have girth exactly g?
credit: G. Exoo and J. Goedgebeur (2019), Question 1; restriction to k ≥ 4 added here
premise_risks: Could be resolved by a single computation once n_6(4) or n_4(6) is pinned down, if a counterexample exists; a positive answer needs a real idea
Restriction k ≥ 4 is ours (the paper's literal question fails for k = 3); vetter should confirm this is the intended question
Rampone 2026 bounds are an unrefereed preprint; not used by the statement
Possible elementary resolution: the vertex-identification argument above settles cases with large diameter; a cleverer local operation might settle all cases
plain: Let n_g(k) be the fewest vertices of a graph that needs k colours and has no cycle shorter than g. Exoo and Goedgebeur asked whether a smallest such graph must have a cycle of length exactly g; equivalently, whether n_g(k) strictly increases with g. For k = 3 this fails (the 5-cycle is smallest for both g = 4 and g = 5), so the question is for k >= 4. The analogous statement for cages is a classical theorem of Erdos and Sachs.
math: Let $n_g(k)=\min\{|V(G)|:\chi(G)=k,\ \mathrm{girth}(G)\ge g\}$. Decide whether $n_g(k)<n_{g+1}(k)$ for all $k\ge 4$ and $g\ge 3$; equivalently, whether every graph with $\chi=k$, girth $\ge g$ and exactly $n_g(k)$ vertices has girth exactly $g$.
review_note: Known: Posed as Question 1 in Exoo–Goedgebeur, 'Bounds for the smallest k-chromatic graphs of given girth', DMTCS 21(3) (2019) #9 (arXiv 1805.06713). Known exact values: n_3(k)=k (K_k), n_4(4)=11 (Grötzsch/Chvátal), n_5(4)=21, n_4(5)=22 (Jensen–Royle); bounds 26 ≤ n_6(4) ≤ 66 (Rampone, arXiv 2608.23652, 2026: 29 ≤ n_6(4) ≤ 64), 30 ≤ n_7(4) ≤ 171, 29 ≤ n_5(5) ≤ 80, 32 ≤ n_4(6) ≤ 40 (Goedgebeur, J. Graph Theory 2020, arXiv 1707.07581). Implied strict cases: n_3(k)<n_4(k) for k ≥ 3 (K_k is the unique smallest), n_4(4)<n_5(4)<n_6(4), n_4(5)<n_5(5).

/-! QED-E056: Do minimum-order k-chromatic graphs of girth at least g have girth exactly g?
Let n_g(k) be the fewest vertices of a graph that needs k colours and has no cycle shorter than g. Exoo and Goedgebeur asked whether a smallest such graph must have a cycle of length exactly g; equivalently, whether n_g(k) strictly increases with g. For k = 3 this fails (the 5-cycle is smallest for both g = 4 and g = 5), so the question is for k >= 4. The analogous statement for cages is a classical theorem of Erdos and Sachs.
Informal statement: Let $n_g(k)=\min\{|V(G)|:\chi(G)=k,\ \mathrm{girth}(G)\ge g\}$. Decide whether $n_g(k)<n_{g+1}(k)$ for all $k\ge 4$ and $g\ge 3$; equivalently, whether every graph with $\chi=k$, girth $\ge g$ and exactly $n_g(k)$ vertices has girth exactly $g$.
Formalization notes:
* Graphs are Mathlib `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` (finite simple graphs on n labelled vertices; every
  finite graph is isomorphic to one). `χ(G) = k` is `G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞)` (Mathlib's
  chromatic number, the least n with a proper n-colouring). Girth uses `G.egirth : ℕ∞`, the
  length of a shortest cycle, `⊤` for forests; "girth ≥ g" is `(g : ℕ∞) ≤ G.egirth` and
  "girth exactly g" is `G.egirth = (g : ℕ∞)`.
* `Good k g G` : χ(G) = k and girth(G) ≥ g. `IsMinimum k g n G` : `Good k g G` and no graph on
  fewer than n vertices is `Good k g`; i.e. n = n_g(k) and G is a smallest such graph.
* `Claim` is the second (equivalent) form: for all k ≥ 4, g ≥ 3, every minimum-order graph with
  χ = k and girth ≥ g has girth exactly g. Equivalence with strict monotonicity: always
  n_g(k) ≤ n_{g+1}(k) (girth ≥ g+1 implies girth ≥ g), and n_g(k) = n_{g+1}(k) iff some
  minimum-order graph for (k,g) has girth ≥ g+1, i.e. girth ≠ g. Graphs with χ = k and girth ≥ g
  exist for all k, g (Erdős 1959), so the sets defining n_g(k) are nonempty and the universal
  statement is not vacuous; this form avoids `sInf` junk values.
* Proving `Claim`: n_g(k) < n_{g+1}(k) for all k ≥ 4, g ≥ 3. Proving `¬Claim`: some k ≥ 4,
  g ≥ 3 and a smallest graph with χ = k, girth ≥ g that has girth > g (so n_g(k) = n_{g+1}(k)).
* Sanity: for k = 3, g = 4 the 5-cycle is a minimum graph of girth 5, which is why k ≥ 4.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE056
noncomputable section

/-- `G` has chromatic number exactly `k` and girth at least `g`. -/
def Good (k g : ℕ) {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞) ∧ (g : ℕ∞) ≤ G.egirth

/-- `G` is a smallest graph with chromatic number `k` and girth at least `g`
(so `n = n_g(k)`). -/
def IsMinimum (k g n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  Good k g G ∧ ∀ m : ℕ, m < n → ∀ H : SimpleGraph (Fin m), ¬ Good k g H

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ k g : ℕ, 4 ≤ k → 3 ≤ g →
    ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), IsMinimum k g n G → G.egirth = (g : ℕ∞)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE056

title: Is a random 5-regular graph 3-colourable?
credit: Diaz, Kaporis, Kemkes, Kirousis, Perez, Wormald (2005/2009); Kemkes, Perez-Gimenez, Wormald
premise_risks: Literature check could not open the 2009 JGT abstract directly; status rests on the 2010 Kemkes-Perez-Gimenez-Wormald statement and absence of later claims. A 2015-2026 result on small-q regular colouring may exist and should be ruled out by the vetter.
Risk that the remaining step is 'just' a rigorous numerical maximisation (lesson 5); but it has been open for 20 years and is a recognised problem.
plain: Choose a graph uniformly at random among all 5-regular graphs on n labelled vertices (n even). Such a graph is known to be 4-colourable with probability tending to 1, and it is known to be 3-colourable with probability tending to 1 provided an explicit four-variable function attains its global maximum at one specific point, which numerics strongly support but nobody has proved. Prove unconditionally that the probability of 3-colourability tends to 1. Degree 5 is exactly where the answer switches: random 4-regular graphs are almost surely 3-colourable, random 6-regular ones almost surely are not.
math: Let $\mathcal G_{n,5}$ be the set of simple 5-regular graphs on $[n]$ ($n$ even), with the uniform measure. Prove $\lim_{n\to\infty,\ n\text{ even}}|\{G\in\mathcal G_{n,5}:\chi(G)\le 3\}|/|\mathcal G_{n,5}|=1$.
review_note: Known: Random 5-regular graphs are a.a.s. 4-colourable (Shi-Wormald, CPC 2007). They are 3-colourable with probability bounded away from 0 if a certain explicit function has a unique maximum at a given point, and a.a.s. 3-colourable under the same hypothesis; extensive numerics support it (Diaz-Kaporis-Kemkes-Kirousis-Perez-Wormald, J. Graph Theory 2009; ESA 2005 version '5-regular graphs are 3-colorable with positive probability'). For general d, chi(G_{n,d}) is a.a.s. k-1 or k (Kemkes-Perez-Gimenez-Wormald, 2010), who note 'we were unable to verify the maximum hypothesis'. Large-k exact results (Coja-Oghlan-Efthymiou-Hetterich, JCTB 2016) do not cover k=3.

/-! QED-E060: Is a random 5-regular graph 3-colourable?
Choose a graph uniformly at random among all 5-regular graphs on n labelled vertices (n even). Such a graph is known to be 4-colourable with probability tending to 1, and it is known to be 3-colourable with probability tending to 1 provided an explicit four-variable function attains its global maximum at one specific point, which numerics strongly support but nobody has proved. Prove unconditionally that the probability of 3-colourability tends to 1. Degree 5 is exactly where the answer switches: random 4-regular graphs are almost surely 3-colourable, random 6-regular ones almost surely are not.
Informal statement: Let $\mathcal G_{n,5}$ be the set of simple 5-regular graphs on $[n]$ ($n$ even), with the uniform measure. Prove $\lim_{n\to\infty,\ n\text{ even}}|\{G\in\mathcal G_{n,5}:\chi(G)\le 3\}|/|\mathcal G_{n,5}|=1$.
Formalization notes: Labelled simple graphs on `[n]` are `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` (loopless,
undirected, no multi-edges — the standard uniform model `G_{n,d}`, not the configuration
model). `G` is 5-regular iff every neighbour set has exactly 5 elements (`Set.ncard`; the
neighbour sets are finite since `Fin n` is). The sets of 5-regular graphs and of
3-colourable 5-regular graphs are subsets of the finite type `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`, so
`Set.ncard` gives their true cardinalities and the ratio is exactly the uniform
probability. χ(G) ≤ 3 is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Colorable 3` (a proper colouring
`Fin n → Fin 3`). Restricting to n = 2m handles parity (no 5-regular graph on an odd
number of vertices); for m ≥ 3 the denominator is positive, and finitely many small m
do not affect the limit. Proving Claim is exactly the unconditional a.a.s.
3-colourability of random 5-regular graphs; ¬Claim says the probability does not tend to 1.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE060
noncomputable section
open Filter Topology

/-- `G` is 5-regular. -/
def IsFiveRegular {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ v : Fin n, (G.neighborSet v).ncard = 5

/-- Proportion of 3-colourable graphs among 5-regular graphs on `n` labelled vertices. -/
def col3Prob (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ({G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) | IsFiveRegular G ∧ G.Colorable 3}.ncard : ℝ) /
    ({G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) | IsFiveRegular G}.ncard : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  Tendsto (fun m : ℕ => col3Prob (2 * m)) atTop (𝓝 1)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE060

title: Is the complete-pivoting growth factor exactly 8 for 8x8 matrices?
credit: A. Edelman & J. Urschel 2023, arXiv:2303.04892 (also Cryer 1968, Gould 1991 for the g_n <= n history)
premise_risks: Exact values g_n are known only for n ≤ 4 (Cryer; Cohen: g_3 = 2.25, g_4 = 4). g_5 = 4.1325 is only conjectured (proved g_5 ≤ 4.84, Edelman–Urschel arXiv:2602.20390, preprint) and g_6 ≥ 5 is only a lower bound. Determining g_7 is therefore much harder than an n ≤ 6 baseline suggests.
plain: The worst-case complete-pivoting growth is known exactly only for n ≤ 4 (values 1, 2, 2.25, 4). For n = 5 the best known value 4.1325 is only conjectured optimal, with proved upper bound 4.84 (Edelman–Urschel, arXiv:2602.20390), and for n = 6 the value 5 is only a lower bound. The value g_8 = 8, attained by Hadamard matrices, is conjectured but unproven, and Hadamard matrices are known not to be optimal at n = 12 and 16. Determine g_7 and decide whether g_8 = 8.
math: With $g_n$ as above (real matrices, complete pivoting), prove or disprove $g_8=8$ (equivalently $g_8\le 8$, since an $8\times8$ Hadamard matrix has growth exactly $8$). Determining $g_7$ (known lower bounds from Edelman–Urschel Table 1) is a separate question, not part of the claim. Background: $g_n$ is known exactly only for $n\le4$; $g_5\le4.84$ (arXiv:2602.20390).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E067: Is the complete-pivoting growth factor exactly 8 for 8×8 matrices?
The worst-case growth factor g_n of Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting is attained value n
by Hadamard matrices for n = 8, and g_8 = 8 is conjectured (Edelman–Urschel). Decide whether g_8 = 8.
Informal statement: With g_n the maximal complete-pivoting growth factor over nonsingular real n×n
matrices, prove or disprove g_8 = 8. (Claim: g_8 ≤ 8; since an 8×8 Hadamard matrix has growth exactly
8, this is equivalent to g_8 = 8. Determining g_7 is a separate question, not part of Claim.)
Formalization notes: After row/column permutations every matrix is in completely pivoted (CP) form:
at each stage m (0-based) the pivot entry (m,m) of the Schur complement has maximal absolute value
in the active block {i, j ≥ m}. `stage A m` is the matrix after eliminating pivots 0..m−1 (entries
with i or j < m are frozen). A is nonsingular iff all pivots are nonzero (given CP). The growth factor
is max_{m,i,j ≥ m} |stage A m i j| / max_{i,j} |a_ij|, and max |a_ij| = |a_00| for CP matrices; all
pivot ties are covered since every tie-breaking produces some CP matrix. `ent` reads entries with ℕ
indices (0 outside range).
Proving `Claim` = g_8 ≤ 8 (hence g_8 = 8). Proving `¬Claim` = an 8×8 CP nonsingular matrix with growth > 8.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE067

/-- Entry with natural-number indices (0 out of range). -/
def ent {n : ℕ} (M : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (i j : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  if h : i < n ∧ j < n then M ⟨i, h.1⟩ ⟨j, h.2⟩ else 0

/-- Matrix after `m` steps of Gaussian elimination without further pivoting. -/
noncomputable def stage {n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) : ℕ → Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ
  | 0 => A
  | m + 1 => Matrix.of fun i j =>
      if m < (i : ℕ) ∧ m < (j : ℕ) then
        stage A m i j - ent (stage A m) (i : ℕ) m * ent (stage A m) m (j : ℕ) / ent (stage A m) m m
      else stage A m i j

/-- `A` is nonsingular and in completely pivoted form. -/
def IsCP {n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ m : ℕ, m < n → ent (stage A m) m m ≠ 0 ∧
    ∀ i j : Fin n, m ≤ (i : ℕ) → m ≤ (j : ℕ) → |stage A m i j| ≤ |ent (stage A m) m m|

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ A : Matrix (Fin 8) (Fin 8) ℝ, IsCP A →
    ∀ m : ℕ, m < 8 → ∀ i j : Fin 8, m ≤ (i : ℕ) → m ≤ (j : ℕ) →
      |stage A m i j| ≤ 8 * |A 0 0|

end OpenProblems.QEDE067
prov_reason: Edelman-Urschel state that g_8 = 8 remains a conjecture.

title: Singularities of the permanental hypersurface
premise_risks: arXiv:2603.15579 (2026 preprint) is listed in refs and may be the source of the current Sing-codimension bounds (6 <= r <= 2n) quoted in M; these are not used by Claim.
plain: The hypersurface where the n x n determinant vanishes has rational singularities, the mildest kind that matters for much of its geometry. Decide whether the hypersurface where the n x n permanent vanishes has rational singularities for every n. Further questions (not part of the formal claim): compute its minimal exponent, a finer measure of how mild a singularity is.
math: Let $X_n=\{\operatorname{per}_n=0\}\subset\mathbb A^{n^2}_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ be Saito's minimal exponent (the smallest root of $b_{\operatorname{per}_n}(-s)/(1-s)$), so that $\operatorname{lct}(\mathbb A^{n^2},X_n)=\min\{1,\tilde\alpha(X_n)\}$ and $X_n$ has rational singularities iff $\tilde\alpha(X_n)>1$, i.e. iff $b_{\operatorname{per}_n}(s)=(s+1)q(s)$ with every root of $q$ less than $-1$. For $n=2$, $X_2$ is a nondegenerate quadric cone in $\mathbb A^4$ and $\tilde\alpha=2$. For $\det_n$ the Bernstein--Sato polynomial is $\prod_{i=1}^n(s+i)$, so $\tilde\alpha(\{\det_n=0\})=2$ for all $n$. Claim: for every $n\ge1$, $X_n$ has rational singularities; formally, some $b(s)=(s+1)q(s)$ with $q\ne0$ and all roots of $q$ of real part $<-1$ satisfies $P(s)\operatorname{per}_n^{s+1}=b(s)\operatorname{per}_n^s$ for some $P(s)\in D_{n^2}[s]$. Prove or disprove (a disproof is an $n$ with $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\le1$). Note: restricting to a generic linear subspace of dimension $r=\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{Sing}(X_n)$ gives an isolated homogeneous singularity, so $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge r/n$. Since $6\le r\le 2n$ is known and $r=2n$ is conjectured, that conjecture would give $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge2$ and rational singularities. Further questions (not part of the formal claim): determine $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ for all $n\ge3$ (in particular for $n=3$); is $\tilde\alpha(X_n)=2$ for all $n$, or does $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\to\infty$?

/-! QED-E068: Singularities of the permanental hypersurface
The hypersurface where the n×n determinant vanishes has rational singularities. Decide whether the
hypersurface where the n×n permanent vanishes has rational singularities for every n (and compute
its minimal exponent).
Informal statement: Let X_n = {per_n = 0} ⊂ 𝔸^{n²}_ℂ and α̃(X_n) Saito's minimal exponent (the
smallest root of b_{per_n}(−s)/(1−s)). X_n has rational singularities iff α̃(X_n) > 1. Decide whether
X_n has rational singularities for every n (Claim: yes). Known: α̃(X_2) = 2; for det_n,
b(s) = ∏_{i=1}^n (s+i), so α̃ = 2. The sharper questions (exact value of α̃(X_n), e.g. n = 3; is
α̃(X_n) = 2 for all n?) are not part of Claim.
Formalization notes: The Bernstein–Sato polynomial b_f is the monic generator of the ideal of
b ∈ ℂ[s] for which there is an operator P(s) = ∑_{j,α} s^j c_{j,α}(x) ∂^α in D_n[s] with
P(s) f^{s+1} = b(s) f^s. Because the evaluation s ↦ m, f^s ↦ f^m is a D-module map to ℂ[x]_f and a
polynomial identity in s holding at all m ∈ ℕ holds identically, this functional identity is
equivalent to the polynomial identities ∑ m^j c_{j,α} ∂^α(f^{m+1}) = b(m) f^m for all m ∈ ℕ, which
is how `IsBMultiple` is stated (∂^α via iterated `MvPolynomial.pderiv`). Saito: rational
singularities ⇔ α̃ > 1 ⇔ b_f(s) = (s+1)q(s) with every root of q < −1. Since b_f divides every
admissible b and (s+1) | b_f, this is equivalent to: some admissible b has the form (s+1)q with q ≠ 0
and all roots of q having real part < −1 (roots of b-functions are negative rationals). n = 0 is
excluded (per_0 = 1 is a unit).

Proving `¬Claim` = for some n, α̃(per_n) ≤ 1 (non-rational singularities).

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE068

/-- The n×n permanent as a polynomial in the n² entries. -/
noncomputable def per (n : ℕ) : MvPolynomial (Fin n × Fin n) ℂ :=
  ∑ π : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), ∏ i : Fin n, MvPolynomial.X (i, π i)

/-- Iterated partial derivative `∂^α g` (the partials commute, so the order is irrelevant). -/
noncomputable def iterPDeriv {σ : Type*} [Fintype σ] [DecidableEq σ] (α : σ →₀ ℕ)
    (g : MvPolynomial σ ℂ) : MvPolynomial σ ℂ :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset σ).toList.foldr
    (fun i acc => (⇑(MvPolynomial.pderiv i : Derivation ℂ (MvPolynomial σ ℂ) (MvPolynomial σ ℂ)))^[α i] acc) g

/-- `b` lies in the Bernstein–Sato ideal of `f`: some `P(s) = ∑ s^j c_{j,α} ∂^α` satisfies
`P(s) f^{s+1} = b(s) f^s`, written via the equivalent identities at every `s = m ∈ ℕ`. -/
def IsBMultiple {σ : Type*} [Fintype σ] [DecidableEq σ] (f : MvPolynomial σ ℂ)
    (b : Polynomial ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (S : Finset (ℕ × (σ →₀ ℕ))) (c : ℕ × (σ →₀ ℕ) → MvPolynomial σ ℂ),
    ∀ m : ℕ,
      ∑ jα ∈ S, MvPolynomial.C ((m : ℂ) ^ jα.1) * c jα * iterPDeriv jα.2 (f ^ (m + 1)) =
        MvPolynomial.C (b.eval (m : ℂ)) * f ^ m

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∃ q : Polynomial ℂ, q ≠ 0 ∧ (∀ r : ℂ, q.IsRoot r → r.re < -1) ∧
    IsBMultiple (per n) ((Polynomial.X + 1) * q)

end OpenProblems.QEDE068
prov_reason: Refs only note that geometric results on permanental hypersurfaces are absent; none asks for the minimal exponent or for rationality.

title: Charge on a Fermat conductor
plain: Put a unit of electric charge on a perfectly conducting solid x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1. Show that the surface charge is thinnest exactly at the six flat points (+-1,0,0),... and thickest exactly at the eight points in the diagonal directions.
math: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4+z^4\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\mu=\rho\,d\sigma$ be its Newtonian (capacitary) equilibrium measure, $\sigma$ surface measure on $\partial K$ ($\rho$ is real-analytic and positive since $\partial K$ is analytic). Prove that $\min_{\partial K}\rho$ is attained exactly at $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$ and $\max_{\partial K}\rho$ exactly at $3^{-1/4}(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$.
